pos: n. (proper name; a Canaanite people descended from Canaan son of Ham)
etymology: Hebrew 'Arqi, the gentilic of Arka, a town on the Phoenician coast north of Tripolis at the foot of Lebanon. The name is formed as the other Canaanite clan-names in Genesis 10 are formed: the place, then the people of the place.
biblical_def: The Arkite is named twice, both times in the roll of Canaan's sons: “And the Hivite, and the Arkite, and the Sinite” (Genesis 10:17), repeated word for word at 1 Chronicles 1:15. He stands eighth in a list of eleven Canaanite peoples, between the Hivite whom Israel would meet in the land and the Sinite of whom nothing further is said. The Arkites settled the northern reach of the Canaanite territory, and their town kept the name for centuries after the clan itself had been absorbed. Two things are worth a reader's notice. The first is that Canaan's line is given in detail at all: the people under the curse of Genesis 9:25 are enrolled by name, fathered, counted, and located, because God numbers even those He will dispossess. The second is the sentence that closes the list: “and afterward were the families of the Canaanites spread abroad” (Genesis 10:18). The spreading was not an accident of migration. It was the providence that set the bounds of their habitation (Acts 17:26) and that fixed the four hundred years before the iniquity of the Amorites was full (Genesis 15:16). The Arkite is a name in a list, and the list is a doctrine: no nation rises or settles outside the government of God.

corruption_summary: The Canaanite clan-lists are treated as late tribal folklore; Scripture gives them as Mosaic record of real peoples under real providence.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 10 is routinely handled as a post-exilic sketch of the world as some later scribe happened to know it, with the clan-names read as back-projections from the geography of a much later century. The dictionary holds Mosaic authorship and the historicity of Noah and his sons. The Arkite is not a literary device; he is a man with descendants, and his town stood where Moses said his people settled.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that providence governs the smallest nation. Eleven Canaanite clans are named, and only a handful ever appear again in the narrative; the rest are known to God and to no one else. He sets the bounds of the habitation of peoples no history records, and He numbers them before He judges them.

pos: n. (proper name; a Canaanite people descended from Canaan son of Ham)
etymology: Hebrew 'Arvadi, the gentilic of Arvad, the island city off the Syrian coast that the Greeks called Aradus. The island is small and waterless, and its men were famous sailors because the sea was all they had.
biblical_def: The Arvadite opens the last line of Canaan's roll: “And the Arvadite, and the Zemarite, and the Hamathite: and afterward were the families of the Canaanites spread abroad” (Genesis 10:18), repeated in short form at 1 Chronicles 1:16. Unlike most of the eleven clans, the Arvadite is heard from again. Ezekiel, setting out the merchant glory of Tyre before he sets out her fall, names them twice over: the men of Arvad were Tyre's mariners, and her soldiers manned the walls. “The inhabitants of Zidon and Arvad were thy mariners” (Ezekiel 27:8). So the dictionary can say of this clan what it cannot say of the Sinite or the Arkite: here is what they became. They became seamen and mercenaries in the service of the richest city on that coast, and when Ezekiel pronounced the word of the LORD against Tyre, the Arvadite went down with the ship he had rowed. That is the shape of a creature's glory when it is hired out to a creature. The island that bred the best sailors in Phoenicia is named in Scripture chiefly to be listed among the hands that served a city God had appointed to sink.

corruption_summary: Tyre's commercial empire is admired as early globalism; Ezekiel names it as a glory God appointed to sink.
corruption_paragraphs: The Phoenician trading world, in which the Arvadite was a hired hand, is commonly presented as an early triumph of commerce and exchange, with Ezekiel 27 read as an admiring inventory. It is not an inventory; it is a lament, and the lament is a sentence. The chapter catalogues the beauty of Tyre precisely so that the reader feels the weight of the words that follow it, and the dictionary reads it as the prophet wrote it.

The principle to recover is that service rendered to a condemned glory shares its end. The Arvadite rowed well and manned the wall faithfully, and it did not save him, because what he served was appointed to fall. “Thy riches, and thy fairs, thy merchandise … shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin” (Ezekiel 27:27). The question Scripture puts to a man's labour is not whether it is skilled but whose it is.

pos: n. (proper name; a people descended from Mizraim son of Ham)
etymology: Hebrew 'Anamim, a plural form of uncertain meaning. The -im ending marks it, like Ludim and Lehabim beside it, as the name of a people rather than of a single man.
biblical_def: The Anamim are named twice and never again: “And Mizraim begat Ludim, and Anamim, and Lehabim, and Naphtuhim” (Genesis 10:13), repeated at 1 Chronicles 1:11. Mizraim is Egypt, and the seven peoples fathered in these two verses are the Egyptian branch of Ham's line. Of the Anamim nothing further is recorded; no prophet names them, no king fights them, no map locates them with certainty. Their whole existence in Scripture is two occurrences of one word, and both times they are in the middle of a list. This is worth stopping over. A reader trained to look for significance will pass such a name quickly, but the Holy Ghost did not think it beneath inspiration to record a people who would never be mentioned again. The genealogies are God keeping account. “These are the families of the sons of Noah, after their generations, in their nations: and by these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood” (Genesis 10:32). The Anamim are in the account because they were in the world, and God wrote down the world He had made and would judge. He will not lose a people, and He will not lose a man.

corruption_summary: Names that go nowhere are read as filler in a late document; they are God's record of peoples no history preserved.
corruption_paragraphs: The unrepeated names of Genesis 10 are often taken as evidence that the chapter is an artificial construction, padded to a schematic count. The dictionary reads them the other way. A forger fills a list with names that do something; a record contains names that do nothing, because the record is of what was, not of what makes a story. The Anamim earn their two lines by having existed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the thoroughness of divine accounting. If a people who never acted in the narrative are written down by name, then no life is beneath God's notice and no obscurity hides a man from His reckoning. “But the very hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matthew 10:30) is the same attribute applied to one person that Genesis 10 applies to a nation.

pos: n. (proper name; a people descended from Mizraim son of Ham)
etymology: Hebrew Kasluchim, of uncertain meaning, with the -im plural that marks a people. The Authorized Version spells it Casluhim at Genesis 10:14 and Casluhim again at 1 Chronicles 1:12.
biblical_def: The Casluhim are named with a parenthesis that makes them matter: “And Pathrusim, and Casluhim, (out of whom came Philistim,) and Caphtorim” (Genesis 10:14). The Chronicler repeats it with the later English name: “(of whom came the Philistines)” (1 Chronicles 1:12). So this otherwise silent Egyptian clan is the recorded ancestor of the nation that would fight Israel from the Judges to David — the people of Gaza and Ashkelon, of Dagon's house, of Goliath of Gath. The note is placed here, in a genealogy written long before the wars, and it tells a reader what Scripture thinks a genealogy is for. It is not decoration; it is the account of how the nations Israel would face came to be, set down before they faced them. Amos and Jeremiah add that the LORD brought the Philistines from Caphtor (Amos 9:7; Jeremiah 47:4), and the dictionary holds both lines without strain: the clan of Casluhim out of Egypt's line, the migration by way of Caphtor, one providence. The enemy God raised up against His people had a father, a homeland, and a departure date, all appointed.

corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 10:14 derives the Philistim from the Casluhim of Egypt's line, while Amos and Jeremiah speak of Caphtor; the two are routinely assigned to different hands and set against each other as rival traditions. The dictionary rejects the method and the conclusion. A people with an ancestor in Egypt's line and a migration by way of Caphtor is one people with a history, and ordinary history contains both a father and a voyage.

The principle to recover is that God appoints the nations that chasten His people. The Philistines are not an accident Israel ran into; their descent is recorded in Genesis and their removal from Caphtor is credited to the LORD by Amos in the same breath as Israel's own exodus. The rod is made before the back that it strikes, and by the same hand.

pos: n. (proper name; a people descended from Dedan, grandson of Abraham by Keturah)
etymology: Hebrew Letushim, plural, from a root carrying the sense of hammering or sharpening — whence the suggestion that the name means smiths or sharpened men. The -im ending marks a people.
biblical_def: The Letushim appear once, in the Keturah genealogy: “And Jokshan begat Sheba, and Dedan. And the sons of Dedan were Asshurim, and Letushim, and Leummim” (Genesis 25:3). This is a line most readers pass over, and it rewards a pause. Abraham took Keturah after Sarah died, and she bore him six sons, and those sons fathered the Arabian peoples — Midian among them. So the father of the faithful is the ancestor not only of Israel through Isaac and of Edom through Esau, but of a wide Arabian world through Keturah. The promise ran through Isaac alone; the natural fatherhood ran everywhere. Scripture is careful to keep these two things from being confused: “in Isaac shall thy seed be called” (Romans 9:7). The Letushim are Abraham's flesh and not Abraham's covenant, and that distinction is the hinge of Romans 9. Being born of the right man is not the same as being born of the promise. The dictionary records the Letushim as what they are — a real people, honourably descended, outside the elect line — because that is precisely the case Paul reasons from.

corruption_summary: Abrahamic descent is treated as itself a standing before God; Scripture distinguishes the flesh of Abraham from the promise to Abraham.
corruption_paragraphs: A great deal of modern religious talk runs on the idea of a shared Abrahamic inheritance, as though natural descent from the patriarch established a common standing with God. Genesis 25 is the text that forbids it. Abraham fathered six sons by Keturah and a wide Arabian posterity through them, and the covenant did not pass to one of them. The Letushim are Abraham's grandchildren's children and strangers to the promise in the same sentence.

The principle to recover is election. “Neither, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all children” (Romans 9:7) is not Paul's innovation; it is his reading of these genealogies. The children of the promise are such by God's free choice, not by blood, and the Letushim stand in the record as the proof that God's grace does not run along the lines that nature draws.

pos: n. (proper name; firstborn son of Joktan, of the line of Shem)
etymology: Hebrew 'Almodad, of uncertain meaning; often read as containing the element mdd, to measure, with a prefixed article, hence the measurer. Nothing in Scripture settles it.
biblical_def: Almodad stands first among the thirteen sons of Joktan: “And Joktan begat Almodad, and Sheleph, and Hazarmaveth, and Jerah” (Genesis 10:26), repeated at 1 Chronicles 1:20. Joktan is of the line of Shem through Arphaxad and Eber, which places Almodad in the blessed line — the line out of which Abraham would come — but on the branch that turns away from it. Eber had two sons: Peleg, through whom the promise runs, and Joktan, whose thirteen sons peopled Arabia. Almodad is the firstborn of the branch that does not carry the covenant. Here is the pattern Scripture repeats until a reader cannot miss it. Shem over Ham and Japheth, Peleg over Joktan, Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Judah over his elder brothers, David over seven older sons. Firstborn by nature is not firstborn by election; God has reserved the right of the firstborn to Himself, and He gives it where He will. “The elder shall serve the younger” (Genesis 25:23). Almodad was his father's eldest and the founder of a people, and the line of promise went the other way.

corruption_summary: Primogeniture is read as the Bible's own rule of inheritance; Scripture overturns it line after line to teach election.
corruption_paragraphs: The genealogies are sometimes read as a straightforward charter of ancient birthright, with the Bible simply reflecting the custom of its age. The text does the opposite with striking regularity. Almodad is a firstborn whose branch carries nothing; Peleg is the brother through whom everything comes. The pattern recurs so often that it is plainly deliberate, and it is deliberate against the custom, not with it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is unconditional election. God's choice is not governed by birth order, merit, or expectation, and the genealogies are where He teaches it before Paul ever argues it. “Not of works, but of him that calleth” (Romans 9:11-12) is the doctrine the lists were written to carry.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Joktan, of the line of Shem)
etymology: Hebrew 'Abima'el, read by most as my father is God — the elements 'ab (father), the suffix -i (my), and 'el (God). A confessional name in an Arabian line.
biblical_def: Abimael is named twice, both times in the roll of Joktan's sons: “And Obal, and Abimael, and Sheba” (Genesis 10:28), with the Chronicler's parallel at 1 Chronicles 1:22, where the brother before him is spelled Ebal. Nothing else is told of him. What is striking is his name. My father is God is a confession, and it stands in a list of Arabian clans on the branch of Shem that the covenant did not follow. The Table of Nations is full of such names — God-bearing names among peoples who would not keep the God whose name they bore. That is not an embarrassment to the record; it is a testimony in it. The knowledge of God was not a late arrival in the world, confined to Israel. It came off the ark with Noah's three sons and it ran out into every branch of the family, and the branches lost it. “Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God” (Romans 1:21). A man named my father is God founding a people that would not worship Him is Romans 1 in a single line of genealogy.

corruption_summary: The knowledge of God is treated as evolving from primitive religion; Scripture has it given at the first and lost by degrees.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard account of religion has men climbing from animism toward monotheism over long ages, with Israel's faith a late achievement. The names in the Table of Nations run against it. God-compounded names appear at the root of the Arabian clans, among peoples whose later religion was idolatrous, which is the signature of a knowledge inherited and then forfeited rather than slowly attained.

The principle to recover is that fallen religion is a descent, not an ascent. Romans 1 states it plainly: men knew God and did not glorify Him, and their foolish heart was darkened. Abimael carried the true God in his name and his descendants did not carry Him in their worship. A right confession in the mouth of a father does not convert a son, and nothing but grace keeps any line in the truth.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Joktan, of the line of Shem)
etymology: Hebrew Diqlah, commonly connected with the Aramaic and Arabic word for the date palm, hence palm grove or place of palms — a name fitting an Arabian oasis people.
biblical_def: Diklah is named twice, in the two parallel rolls of Joktan's sons: “And Hadoram, and Uzal, and Diklah” (Genesis 10:27), and “Hadoram also, and Uzal, and Diklah” (1 Chronicles 1:21). Nothing more is said of him. If the traditional reading of the name is right, he is the palm-grove, and his people took their name from the one thing a desert country prizes: a place where water stands and trees grow. That is how most of the clans of Joktan are named — from a well, a grove, an enclosure, a stretch of ground. Scripture does not disdain so plain a derivation. The whole of Genesis 10 is a record of men settling land, and land is where God puts men. “When the most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people” (Deuteronomy 32:8). Diklah's grove was given, not found. The dictionary notes it because a reader who learns to see appointment in the division of the earth has learned something that governs how he reads the rest of the Bible, and how he holds his own portion of ground.

corruption_summary: The settlement of peoples is read as migration and conquest only; Scripture names it as an inheritance divided by the Most High.
corruption_paragraphs: The spread of the nations after the flood is commonly explained wholly in terms of pressure, climate and conquest — peoples going where they could. Scripture grants the ordinary means and names the hand behind them. Deuteronomy 32:8 says the Most High divided and separated and set the bounds, and Paul repeats it at Athens as the ground on which God may be sought.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a people's land is a stewardship, not a possession seized. Diklah's palms were allotted. So is every acre a man farms and every house he keeps, and the LORD who divided the inheritance of the nations may redivide it, as Israel learned in the year her own land was taken from her.

pos: n. (proper name; a people descended from Dedan, grandson of Abraham by Keturah)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ashshurim, plural. The form resembles Asshur, the name of Assyria, but the Keturah clan is distinct from the Assyrian nation of Shem's line; the resemblance is of sound, not of descent.
biblical_def: The Asshurim are named once: “And Jokshan begat Sheba, and Dedan. And the sons of Dedan were Asshurim, and Letushim, and Leummim” (Genesis 25:3). They belong to the Keturah genealogy, the record of the children Abraham fathered after Sarah's death, and they are three generations down from him — Abraham, Jokshan, Dedan, and then these three clans. Their name must not be confused with Asshur the son of Shem (Genesis 10:22), from whom Assyria took its name; these are Arabian desert clans of Abraham's flesh, not the empire that would one day carry Israel away. The chapter in which they stand is a careful piece of divine bookkeeping. Genesis 25 settles Abraham's whole posterity before the narrative narrows to Isaac: Ishmael's twelve princes are listed, Keturah's six sons and their clans are listed, and then the account turns to the son of promise and never looks back. God closes the books on the branches before He follows the line. “But unto Isaac's sons Abraham gave gifts” is not what the text says; it says Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac and sent the others away with gifts (Genesis 25:5-6). The Asshurim are honourably provided for and honourably dismissed.

corruption_summary: The non-elect branches of Abraham's house are read as unjustly excluded; Scripture shows them provided for and distinguished.
corruption_paragraphs: Election is often protested as though it left the non-chosen robbed. Genesis 25 answers the protest with a detail: Abraham gave gifts to the sons of the concubines and sent them away eastward, and Isaac received the inheritance. The Asshurim were not cheated of a covenant that was never theirs; they were given what was theirs to have. God's particular grace to one line is not an injustice to another.

The principle to recover is the difference between the children of the flesh and the children of the promise. “They which are the children of the flesh, these are not the children of God” (Romans 9:8). The Asshurim stand in the record as Abraham's flesh, and the record is careful to say so, because the whole doctrine of free grace depends on the line being drawn where God drew it and not where blood would draw it.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Dishon, of the Horite line in Edom)
etymology: Hebrew Keran, of uncertain meaning; possibly connected with a root for a lyre or for lamb, but nothing in the text settles it.
biblical_def: Cheran is named twice, both times last in a short list: “And these are the children of Dishon; Hemdan, and Eshban, and Ithran, and Cheran” (Genesis 36:26), repeated at 1 Chronicles 1:41. He belongs not to Esau's line but to the Horites, the people who held mount Seir before Edom took it. Genesis 36 is a remarkable chapter: it records Esau's generations, and then, without apology, the generations of the Horites whom Esau's sons dispossessed and absorbed. The dispossessed are written down by name. This is the habit of Scripture that modern reading most often misses. A chapter concerned to show how Edom came to be does not quietly drop the people Edom displaced; it names their chiefs, their sons, and their daughters. Cheran is one such name — a man of a vanished people, preserved in the record of the people who replaced him. “He hath remembered his covenant for ever, the word which he commanded to a thousand generations” (Psalm 105:8) is said of God's people; but the God who remembers a thousand generations of His own has not forgotten the Horites either, and He wrote their names in the book that outlasted them.

corruption_summary: Displaced peoples are assumed erased from the biblical record; Genesis 36 enrolls the Horites whom Edom replaced.
corruption_paragraphs: It is often said that the Bible is written only by and for the victors, with the conquered left out. Genesis 36 is a direct counter-instance. The chapter that establishes Edom's pedigree takes a long passage to enroll the Horite chiefs and their sons by name, and Deuteronomy 2:12 states the displacement plainly rather than hiding it. Cheran survives in Scripture because Scripture kept him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the candour of the inspired record. It tells of dispossession it does not flatter, including Israel's own, and it keeps the names of those who lost. A book that preserves the genealogy of a people it reports as destroyed is not propaganda; it is testimony, and its candour is part of why it may be trusted.
